title: Fronted phrases
note: Fronted phrase + no inversion - the B1 repair rung between a1_word_order (SVO) and c1_clefts_fronting (deliberate fronting). Built 2026-08-20 from Tomas's error log ('for me is it'); the same fault is general Czech transfer. Three strands x 12: adverbial opener + real subject, opener + it/there in the subject seat, opener that is a whole clause. Order_click is the point; quiz distractors are the inverted and subject-dropped forms students actually produce.

cards.title: What it is
cards.body: English lets you put a phrase at the front of a sentence - a time, a place, a point of view. What it never does is swap the subject and the verb because of it. The subject-verb core stays exactly as it was.
cards.body_cz: Angličtina dovolí dát na začátek věty čas, místo nebo hledisko. Nikdy kvůli tomu ale neprohodí podmět a sloveso. Jádro podmět-sloveso zůstává beze změny.
points: A comma after a longer opener is normal
Everything after the comma is an ordinary sentence

cards.title: Why Czech pushes the other way
cards.body: Czech puts the verb straight after the fronted phrase: *Pro mě je to těžké.* Copy that rhythm into English and you get "For me is it difficult" - the commonest Czech word-order fault there is.
cards.body_cz: Čeština dává sloveso hned za úvodní frázi: Pro mě je to těžké. Když ten rytmus přenesete do angličtiny, vznikne „For me is it difficult“ - nejčastější česká chyba ve slovosledu.

cards.title: The subject seat
cards.body: After the opener something must sit in the subject seat. When there is no real subject, English uses **it** - or **there** when you are saying that something exists.
cards.body_cz: Po úvodní frázi musí být místo podmětu obsazené. Když skutečný podmět není, angličtina použije it - nebo there, když říkáte, že něco existuje.

rows: There is necessary to have good English.
**It is** necessary to have good English.
After the meeting is a lot of work.
After the meeting, **there is** a lot of work.

points: See **It as subject** for the full it / there drill

cards.title: Openers that are clauses
cards.body: The same rule holds when the opener is a whole clause. Both halves keep subject before verb - including the opener itself.
cards.body_cz: Totéž platí, když je na začátku celá věta. Obě části si drží pořadí podmět-sloveso, včetně té úvodní.

rows: When born our second son, we moved.
When **our second son was born**, we moved.

cards.title: The safer sentence
cards.body: Fronting is optional. If the opener is short and you are unsure, put it back where it came from - the plain order is always available and often the better sentence.
cards.body_cz: Fronting není povinný. Když si nejste jistí, dejte úvodní frázi zpátky na konec - základní pořadí je vždycky k dispozici.
points: For me, it is difficult. → **It is difficult for me.**
In Prague, we have an office. → **We have an office in Prague.**

cards.title: The exception, for later
cards.body: English does invert after a fronted phrase in a small set of formal patterns - *Never have I seen...*, *Not only did she...*. That is a deliberate B2/C1 effect with its own rules, not the everyday case here. See **Inversion**.
cards.body_cz: V malé skupině formálních vazeb angličtina po úvodní frázi opravdu prohazuje pořadí (Never have I seen...). To je záměrný efekt na úrovni B2/C1, ne běžný případ.

cards.title: Practice focus
cards.body: Order: click the words into a correct English sentence. Quiz and Type: supply what follows the opener - subject + verb, in that order.
cards.body_cz: Order: seřaďte slova do správné anglické věty. Quiz a Type: doplňte, co následuje po úvodní frázi - podmět + sloveso, v tomto pořadí.
